items.body: When one is asked to summarize one’s travels, for Verónica Cerrotta a month in the city of Valparaíso and a pair of festival appearances, one may respond in varying fashions. On Álbum de Viaje, Cerrotta offers a pair of side-long soundscapes; one travels through time and space, while the other condenses time. Together, they offer complementary ways of preserving experience through sound. The pieces of “Valparaíso” were collected as one might collect souvenirs: scrap by scrap, sound by sound. At first there is only a background hum, then the tapping and swirling of solid objects: metal, plastic, concrete? Then the first confident splash, accompanied by the sounds of workers by the sea. Traffic builds as the city comes to life. A child is playing in the distance, along with whistles and a brass symphony of undulating horns. If only all traffic were this way, offering something good along with the bad! The brass gives way to tinkling wind chimes, as one imagines the amalgamation of all the chimes from all the houses, ringing in time. The tin sound of a radio breaks through, the worker’s best friend. A massive wave bisects the composition, prefacing the appearance of sea lions and hungry gulls. As the velocity of the waves decreases, so does the biophony. A plane passes overhead, seemingly close. Church bells toll, marking time for the dockworkers. Glorious rain on tin roofs creates a percussionist’s paradise, followed by found objects used as percussion. Cerrotta has turned her idyllic month into a photo album of sound. “Otras Ciudades” takes a different approach, traveling backwards in time as it traces two festival appearances with Cerrotta’s band a.hop. “The world is ending,” an unidentified narrator begins; but in truth it is not; it is instead unwinding. A happy get-together in Berlin is accompanied by more church bells, louder than before: in this instance the chronic marker is questioned as the very concept of time is challenged. Small groups of people mill about; a dog barks; the bells continue to ring. The soundscape will eventually move through nations as well as days. The second movement begins with footsteps, first on solid ground and then seemingly through fallen leaves. Who can resist a good leaf patch? Even the nearby birds are laughing. Snippets of conversation are heard, dissolving into patches of music, a local musician, and even more bells. A barge approaches, sounding a warning. The water in this piece connects to the water in the first. Ironically, in concert people come to hear Cerrotta, where Cerrotta shares what she has heard, which in some cases may be the sounds created by audience members themselves. Viaje is a word with various interrelated meanings: trip, travel, journey. Álbum de Viaje honors all three. In the 17th minute, one hears the sound of what may be a map unfolding: a tactile way to approach travel. By the end, because the chronology is reversed, Cerrotta has not returned home, but remembered who she was before she left, when the map was just a map and each sound now heard was only a sound imagined. (Richard Allen)

items.body: A really enjoyable eerie, isolationist and wistful electronic ambient release with enough ideas and well-designed textures to enthrall the listener. Emotional despair collides with surreal, unearthly motifs Meldrop by IUGA   Unexplained Sounds Group, Eighth Tower and ZeroK represent a small community of labels headed by Raffaele Pezzella (alias Sonologyst) and which participate actively in the promotion of spaced-out/experimental and post-industrial ambient music. Each label has its own field of specialization. Unexplained Sounds Group easily represents the most abstract and conceptually inclined sonic soundscapes of the three mentioned above, delivering a body of work from confirmed projects to promising acts coming from a vast array of cultural and geographical cradles. IUGA is a totally new project; few informations are available online, but the least we can say is that it is a welcoming addition to the label’s usual sound signature. As illustrated by the cover artwork, the listener is invited to be immersed in a profound, deep, then isolated and menacing, harrowing, brainy musical bath where emotional despair collides with surreal, unearthly motifs. The atmospheres are partly soothing, darkly meditative, but also uncanny, foreboding, ghoulish. Massive hypnotic drone textures interact with broken electronic signals, technological derelicts, echoing concrete sounds and cyber-like flowing movements. The album also plays with various pitches, filters and sonic sound-expanding techniques. A track such as “Aspis” develops impeccable and transportive otherworldly tones. The whole thing will lead you to a dystopian futuristic world or to some long-forgotten eras. Some parts admit more soothing sequences, such as the repetitive and nebulous “Porcupine Quills.” The closing theme is a dynamic, eroded, meandering, then progressively corrosive, distorted ambient epilogue for looping textures and processing chains of micro-sounds: slow movements evolve through an infinitely static structure. Somewhere between Bad Sector, Kristoff Oustad, Vestigial, Reutoff, The Haxan Cloak—with a fancy for cryptic, strange and molecular sound explorations that won’t deny pioneering figures in bleak industrial/power electronics. A really enjoyable eerie, isolationist and wistful electronic ambient release with enough ideas and well-designed textures to enthrall the listener. Meldrop is available on Unexplained Sounds Group. items.body: EMEFE spent nine years watching “Sun Spat” live a life they never planned for it. Written by saxophonist Jas Walton and tucked into the band’s 2015 self-titled album as a deep cut, it was never released as a single, and never backed by any promotional machinery. It just moved. Slowly, through streaming algorithms and word of mouth, the track gathered millions of plays, a quiet breakout for a New York horn-led ensemble that had already gone on indefinite hiatus in 2016. The live version captured here, “Sun Spat Live in Brooklyn,” was recorded at The Sultan Room in Bushwick and filmed by Isaac Gillespie. It appears on the band’s new four-track EP Sun Spat 2026, released 22 May. The performance features a nine-piece lineup: Walton on tenor sax, Lynn Ligammari on baritone sax, Julie Acosta on trumpet, Aani Kisslinger on trombone, Miles Francis on drums, Doug Berns on bass, Jake Pinto on keys, Harry Terrell and Tim Allen on guitars, and Javier Ramos on congas and percussion. Mixed and mastered by Shiftee, the Brooklyn-based mix engineer and two-time DMC World Champion, with live recording by Sharif Mekawy. EMEFE formed in 2009 when Francis, then a 19-year-old freshman at NYU who had just joined Antibalas and was studying under afrobeat pioneer Tony Allen, assembled a group of jazz school classmates drawn to Fela Kuti’s rhythmic architecture. Over time, the band folded in funk, new wave and neo-soul, keeping the horn section as the ensemble’s lead voice and Berns’s bass as its anchor. Members went on to tour with Mark Ronson, David Byrne, The Roots and Sharon Jones during the hiatus years, but “Sun Spat” kept pulling people in. When EMEFE reconvened for their 2025 album FORWARD and played sold-out rooms, Francis asked the crowd who was seeing the band for the first time. Most of the room put their hands up. But when the band played “Sun Spat,” every one of them already knew the words. items.body: Review by TenYearsAfter — The idea for this musical project came from Flamborough Head's keyboard player Edo Spanninga by accident when he tested some recording equipment in order to record Seventies styled music as a fun-project. Eventually Edo was so excited about the results that he recruited fellow Flamborough Head member Eddie Mulder (guitars and bass) and Odyssice drummer Menno Boomsma to make an album. The name Trion is a contraction of the words 'trio' and 'Mellotron', simply because the band is a trio and because Edo used only Mellotron samples (flute, oboe, strings, organ, cello, vibe and choir) for his keyboard sound on this album. The trio had total freedom to exchange ideas and to work on the arrangements.In 2003 the Dutch trio Trion released their debut CD entitled Tortoise, in 2007 followed by Pilgrim and in 2013 by Funfair Fantasy, all wonderful symphonic prog albums, layered with beautiful Mellotron samples and moving guitarwork. These 3 albums were received very well on Prog Archives by the progheads of Mellotron drenched symphonic rock. In between Colossus (Finnish Progressive Rock Society) invited Trion to contribute to the 2-CD The Spaghetti Epic (featuring progrock bands from all over the world). Trion was OK and delivered the epic Frank. This composition can be found on their second album, in a re-arranged version (close to 23 minutes).And now, anno 2026, Trion's new album entitled Terra Tiempo, after a 13-year hiatus. It contains 12 tracks, mostly instrumental (only two with vocals), ranging between 3 and 7 minutes. The sound is very melodic and harmonic, rooted in the 70s symphonic rock tradition, with a pleasant variety and an own musical touch.Terra Tiempo: The first composition delivers flowing shifting moods and tasteful work on keyboards (from sparkling Grand piano to majestic Mellotron violins) and guitar (from sensitive to fiery), topped with a fluent and dynamic rhythm section. Focus and Camel come to my mind but Trion also presents lots of interesting musical ideas. I notice that the trio sounds as a four-piece formation and has matured during the years.Nautilus: The music alternates between dreamy, a slow rhythm, a tight mid-tempo beat (intro and outro) and bombastic outbursts, embellished with a wide range of keyboards (orchestral, church organ, Hammond, Mellotron flute, synthesizer flights) and wonderful, very moving guitar work.The Return Of Jemetrion: After an intro with tender piano the music turns into a slow rhythm with Mellotron violins, sensitive electric guitar (including slide), floods of Hammond and synthesizer runs. What a wonderful interplay between the guitar and keyboards, firmly rooted in the 70s symphonic rock tradition (from Focus to Camel). Next a dreamy interlude with Mellotron flute and a spacey synthesizer solo, and in the end the sensitive electric guitar play returns.Aftertouch: After flashy synthesizer flights, Hammond and powerful drum beats a slow rhythm follows, featuring a blend of Mellotron violins, synthesizer runs, soaring Hammond and moving guitar runs, it sounds very dynamic and compelling. Halfway slide guitar, blended with lush Mellotron violins and Hammond, and topped with Mellotron flute work.Melloreed: First military drums, a spacey synthesizer sound and soaring Mellotron violins, then a slow rhythm featuring tender synthesizer flights, an accordion sound and Mellotron violins, backed by a deep bass sound and slow drum beats. It sounds as very tasteful and elaborate symphonic rock, with hints of 76-77 Genesis.Intermission: This short track starts in a dreamy climate with soaring synthesizers, the atmosphere is a bit melancholical, then tender piano play, pretty intense.Red Dust: The intro features an impressive choir, taken from a 1938 Mattheus Passion vinyl record! Then a slow rhythm with an electric guitar that rocks, fiery and howling. Next spacey synthesizers and Mellotron flute, blended with dreamy English vocals, a bit fragile. The emotional undertone is emphasized by the soaring Mellotron violins, moving electric guitar and slow synthesizer runs. This track features vocal parts done by drummer Menno Boomsma.Far Away: In this track Trion showcases its variety and musical ideas with folky acoustic guitar, subtle assorted percussion (like Neil Peart from Rush) and majestic Mellotron violins, in a slow rhythm, simply beautiful.One: This excellent composition alternates between dreamy, a slow rhythm and bombastic, what a tension and dynamics, wonderfully coloured with tasteful and varied work on keyboards (lush Mellotron violins, synthesizer flights, orchestral keyboards and tender Mellotron flute) and guitar, from intense slide to moving runs. The rhythm-section does a good job, from subtle to powerful.Growing Clouds: This short piece contains dreamy and intense interplay between acoustic guitar and fragile vocals again done by Boomsma.Paradox Groove: First an exciting contrast between a soaring synthesizer (phaser sound) sound and rock guitar, backed by tight drum beats. Then a slow rhythm featuring sensitive and distorted electric guitar, blended with spacey synthesizers. Another fine example of the interesting musical ideas on this album.Space For Everybody: First a slow rhythm with jazzy electric piano and a flashy synthesizer sound, then a wonderful electric guitar solo with howling runs. Halfway an acceleration (evoking Camel) featuring moving guitar and powerful Hammond, in a mid-tempo beat. The final part delivers first a slow rhythm, embellished with Hammond, synthesizer flights and awesome Mellotron choirs, then another moving guitar solo. In the end the music fades away with Hammond, Mellotron and guitar, a subtle goodbye from the band.After Elements Of Hope by Glorious Wolf (Ruud Dielen project) and E.D.O. (solo project Edo Spanninga) with The Past Is A Foreign Country here is another strong and interesting new Dutch prog album, thumbs up for Trion!

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — SOLAR BLOOMS is the three piece band of David Margalitadze (vocals, guitar), Andrew Shvai (guitar),Serj Jaroschuck (bass) and Paul Vesnianka (drums) from the Ukrainian city of Lutsk that formed in2019 and spent five years crafting its debut release AKH�LI DZ�LIS DABAD�BA which translates as"Birth Of A New Power" in the Georgian language. This somewhat hard to classify progressive rockalbum is the band's debut and features a blend between psychedelic rock, hard rock, stoner metal andwhat to me sounds a bit like neo-prog at times. Loose comparisons yield hints of Porcupine Treestyled atmospheric effects along with Riverside-like heavier rock, Anekdoten also comes to mind aswell as emotive vocals more akin to neo-prog.This debut was released in 2024 and features nine tracks that add up to 49 1/2 minutes. Pushing playand simply listening to the first opening sounds of "Solid Soil" one may believe they just initiateda post-rock type of album with hints of Pink Floyd and indeed many of the intros do share those samecharacteristics but SOLAR BLOOMS has become adept at seamless blending of prog styles that for 2024may sound a bit dated as this Porcupine Tree production type of album was most prominent in theearly 2000s but nevertheless SOLAR BLOOMS offers enough variety and delivers it all in such atasteful manner that it's really hard to complain about any sort of retro effect. The track quicklybecomes enveloped by thick atmospheric backing and English lyrics which really give no indicationthis band emerged from the Slavic nation of Ukraine.The catchy hook-infused compositions continue with the guitar-centric riffing of "Rays Of Sun"however this more tender approach may remind a bit of the 80s new romantic singing style of bandslike Spandau Ballet more than a prog band but then the harder rock aspects kick in and things shifta bit to a more melodic style of prog with more elegant singing. "Tombstone Cities" begins much likea neo-prog style with arpeggiated guitar sweeps and thick atmospheres before emotive vocals deliverythe tale du jour. The track doesn't remain firmly in that style and the mood shifts to morerambunctious with heavy guitar more in the heavier Porcupine Tree camp or bands like OSI for thatmatter yet atmospheric touches remain a main staple of the musical flow. "Deliverance" continues theheaviness while "Space Will Remain" delivers a more space rock approach but not anything remotelyFloydian. Same goes for "Indifference."My favorite track on board is the feisty "Defeated" which is the heaviest and fastest on board andis the one track that qualifies as bonafide metal with fiercely strummed guitar works and pummelingpercussion however even at this agitated mode, vocalist David Margalitadze's vocal style remainscool and calculated belying the thundering din underpinning it all. "Transform Us" is anothercrunchy rocker but less emphatic skirting on mid tempo but features a wily variation of rhythmicchanges. The closing title track is the lengthiest on board at over nine minutes and features mostsophisticated build up and crescendo effect of any track on board. Once again kicking off more as apost-rock type of style slowly oozes into a more rock oriented atmospheric heavy space rock styleending the album on a very satisfying note. This album was quite effective on the first exposure andholds up over repeated listens. The band members deliver admirably and the production is perfect.While influences are abound the band sounds unique and demonstrates a sense of maturity that wasunexpected.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — While ITOIZ was one of the most popular acts to emerge from the prog rock boom from the Basquespeaking region of Spain in the late 70s, this band actually extended its career far beyond its 1974formation and made it all the way to 1988 before disbanding but like virtually every other Spanishprogger to play catch up during a small window of time that emerged after the collapse of the Francoregime and the end of the prog window closing at the end of the 1970s, ITOIZ too had to simplify itsmusic to join the world of radio friendly pop music although the band continued to performexclusively in the Basque language. Following its 1978 self-titled debut the band had one more progrelease in them with its second album EZEKIAL before succumbing to pressures of the marketplace.This sophomore release expanded the core five members to include a three additional musicians thatadded the violin, mandolin, saxophone, cuatro and extra piano. In addition to that an additionalvocalist and children's choir. This was the band's most acclaimed release.As the title suggests this is indeed a concept album referring to the prophet EZEKIAL which thealbum uses as a template for related biblical themes. The album followed the trend of Basque progacts eschewing the Andalusian flamenco influences and infusing the local folk flavors with elementsof progressive rock and jazz. The flute aspects evoked the fluttering tenderness of a classic JethroTull album while the dreamy pastoral folk passages seemed more inspired by Genesis or Camelespecially with the thick atmospheric keyboards adding layers of dreamy ambience however musicallythe melodic touches were fueled by Basque folk with the contrast emerging in more powerful guitarrock. The album features eight tracks with each tackling a different theme based on the prophet. Thealbum runs about 37 minutes and displayed a much more ambitious last hoorah for its prog leaningsbefore plummeting into the simplified pop arena devoid of any such complexities. The album is a lot mellower than even the mellow debut with its acoustic-fueled folk aspects as theunderpinning that finds the world of rock and jazz invited over to have a conversation. The opening'Ezekielen Prophezia' sets the stage with a standard introduction to the flavors of the debut alongwith the addition of a violin. As the tracks continue the saxophone is added and by the third trackwe find a strange mix of symphonic keyboards melding with a Tull-ish flute flurry and a smooth jazzsaxophone joining in which to my ears is the weakest part. Imagine if you will Kenny G joining Cameland Tull for a jam and you'd not be too far off. The album continues these same characteristics withvocalist Juan Carlos P'rez delivering the same somewhat underwhelming vocals that were present onthe debut. The fourth track simply titled 'Ezekiel' features the children's choir along with asimple campfire type of guitar accompaniment. It's a bit campy actually and sounds rather out ofplace. For my ears the first half of the album sounds rather clunky without any true cohesiveness to asupposedly concept album and the musical deliveries are very steeped in progressiveness. It's notreally until the fifth track 'Ezekielen Ikasgaia' where the albums comes to life with Itziar Egileorpicking up vocal duties which makes me wonder why she wasn't the lead vocalist on the whole album asshe blows the dude away big time however once again the Kenny G soft sax parts rub me the wrong wayespecially with the psychedelic organs by their side since it all seems to cancel each other for theproper effect. The best tracks for me are the ending ones. 'Ezekielen Ametsa' at last offers somemore interesting song structures and vocal performances (by the girl) which basically continues intothe following track 'Ezekielen Erantzuna.' Here the band sounds more in sync and the elements geltogether much better which is thankfully features less sax interruptions. Overall this is a decentalbum but too many irritating aspects for me to warm up to. So many other better Basque bands IMHOso i'm not sure why this one has appealed to so many more than the rest.

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — I've already posted my review of Flea's Topi O Uomini, which I enjoyed very much, so I was excited to see that the band members had another project by the name of Etna. And even better, it was a jazz fusion record, and I do love me some good Italian fusion. So, going into this, I already had some high expectations, and to be honest, I think they were indeed met. This record has that classic, fast-paced, and energetic sound that I love about jazz fusion, never leading me off an edge and keeping my ears open right up until the end. Sure, maybe not the most original music out there, but some strong tunes nevertheless! The album cover also stood up to the musical performance in terms of quality, displaying a provoking collage of various exploding colors and indistinguishable yet intriguing images. Francesco Pennisi did a great job with the art here. As it turns out, his brother, Carlo, played guitar and mandolin in the record. The other musicians include Antonio Marangolo on keyboards, Elio Volpini on bass, and Agostino Marangolo on drums. The record opens with the shortest song on the album (being only a little under 4 minutes long), but I think it does a great job at representing this quirky and fun music that is present throughout the entire album. It may be a little lacking in energy, however, and is the weakest song on this project. However, the material just gets better from here on out. Pretty much every song here is amazing and incorporates very interesting and well-put-together aspects of the band members' capabilities. It's very reminiscent of Arti E Mestieri, weaving and bending across these jams of intricate arrangements that twist every few seconds while simultaneously expanding into every moment. It feels very powerful the way they have their tight grooves kicking throughout the whole record and songs like South East Wind, Golden Idol (which is also the longest piece on the album), and Sentimental Lewdness. Don't be fooled by all this energy though, as the band knows how to make good use of dynamics and includes laid-back and relaxed bits to refresh the listener in a way, sometimes being things such as ambient improvisation and soundscapes, which I find really interesting. In conclusion, Etna is a lovely little record that fits nicer with the Italian fusion and wider Rock Progressivo Italiano scene. Not an essential per se, but definitely a good second-tier album for fans of that type of stuff or those who are generally just looking for more high energy and exciting music along the same lines as Mahavishnu Orchestra or Jean Luc Ponty (but without the violin, unfortunately). This is, in my eyes, deserving of a very strong 4.25/5.

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — Riccardo Zappa's debut album, by the name of Celestion, is another one of the heavily unknown albums I pulled from various conversations with friends and colleagues alike about the more underground artists of Rock Progressivo Italiano. It was much more on the lighter and delicate side of the spectrum, with classical Italian folk music playing a big part in the overall makeup of this project. Overall, it's pretty good, with a little too much meandering here and there, but I can still tolerate it. It seems like it had a few too many upbeat, rocking sections than I would've liked, but it was enjoyable nonetheless. Moving on, when it comes to the other musicians on this project, the personnel includes Vince Tempera on keyboards, Julius Farmer on bass, Ottavio Corbellini on drums, and George Aghedo on percussion. All guitars, vocals, and (from what I can tell) songwriting are done by Ricardo. The music can feel a little dull at points, not bringing much interesting nor original material to the table. Sure, it's good, and there are some cool moments of jazzy prog and jamming going on that (admittedly) sometimes ruin the mood of the softer acoustic sections, but for the most part I would say it's quite forgettable. The production also didn't help, as I didn't enjoy the actual sound of the record. I feel like out of the five songs that only add up to around thirty-four minutes of runtime, the opening composition and longest of the bunch, Frammenti, is the strongest. It does a good job at introducing us to the sound we'll be having for the majority of the album, that being mysterious folk bits, sometimes mixed in with vibrant ambience, and then short bursts of fun rock music sprinkled in every few minutes or so. I feel like what this album does get right, however, is the soothing and dreamy feeling of some of the music here. It can flow into a hazy state for a while and float the listener along, but sometimes it can feel inconsistent, and I feel like this album would've actually been better if it was more acoustic-based instead of exciting, though at times tension-breaking, rock music slips into the cracks. Other than that, the songs can go in one ear and out the other and don't really stick that much. In conclusion, this will be one of the weaker records from the Rock Progressivo Italiano scene in my opinion. Without keeping an interesting sound going, I find it hard to really enjoy this record or give anything above a light 3/5.

Electro Aggression Records has also posted the YouTube previews “Broken Mirror album snippets”, “Fight or Suffer | EAR 019 preview” and “Reject | EAR 019 preview”. About T.A.N.K. Reinhard Hüber, who has a 1990s German punk background, launched T.A.N.K. in Dessau in 2001. The name stands short for “Taktischer Angriff (auf’s) Nervenkostüm”. The first live appearance took place at the first Electric Tremor Festival in Dessau on March 22, 2002. The self-released “T.A.N.K.” EP landed in 2002. It was followed by the debut album “Musica Denaturale” on Ars Electrique in 2003. In 2011, the project contributed “Game of Men” to the 4CD set “Old School Electrology Volume One”. In the Electro Aggression Records orbit, Hüber also turned up through remix work connected to R010R and Synaptic Defect before “Broken Mirror” moved into the foreground as the next full album. “Broken Mirror” is be the project’s third album holding 19 tracks.

items.body: Kristof Bathory brought Dawn Of Ashes to life in 2000. The first albums by this American artist were released through the now-defunct Noitekk label, immediately grabbing listeners by the throat with their raw, icy, and uncompromising blend of Dark-Electro and Aggrotech. More than twenty years later, this musical visionary can look back on a rich and successful career during which the project evolved through several distinct eras — from its original Dark-Electro-driven sound to Industrial-Metal, before ultimately returning to its Electronic roots on the previous opus, now infused with the Cinematic influences Bathory also explores in his solo work. With over two decades of dark visions, sonic aggression, and constant musical transformation, Kristof Bathory remains one of the most uncompromising figures within the scene. With “Anatomy Of Suffering,” released on Metropolis this spring, he not only confirms his return to a more Electronic approach, but also delivers a remarkably mature work in which he continues his meticulous exploration of mental anguish and psychological suffering. Dawn Of Ashes has always remained a project with a striking visual identity, perfectly aligned with the disturbing themes it addresses. As a listener, you can feel the suffering permeating every aspect of the project, balanced by a profound artistic vision and emotional depth. Time for a conversation with the artist himself. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Dawn Of Ashes interview Q: What does Dawn Of Ashes mean to you after more than a quarter of a century of existence, and what comes to mind spontaneously when you look back, even just for a moment? And, with the knowledge and experience you have today, what would you like to say to the young Kristof Bathory of the year 2000? Kristof: Dawn Of Ashes is an ongoing, evolving reflection of myself, revealing the different phases of my maturity and growth through both the music and the lyrics. There are things I can unearth from the past and give new purpose to in the present, and there are other things better left buried deep within the tomb. If I could speak to my younger self, early Kristof, I would tell him to make wiser decisions and to have patience before making impulsive choices. Q: Your new album “Anatomy Of Suffering” seems to leave little room for interpretation, but could you still tell us a bit more about it? What is the backstory of this opus, how personal is it, and how did you translate it into music? Kristof: “Anatomy Of Suffering” is a descent into the mind of suicide, pain, and the grotesque rot that festers within as a result of severe mental corrosion. It is both a deeply personal expression and a means of connecting with those who endure this same inner decay. Q: Psychological suffering has long been a recurring theme in your work, and I sometimes wonder how introspective and therapeutic music can be. Could it not also lead to even more suffering? What fascinates me is how obscure, dark, and even destructive themes can culminate in an artistic peak. How do you perceive that process? Kristof: I suppose it all depends on how you interpret it and how you absorb it. Art is subjective—it can either reflect destruction or illuminate a path toward blissfulness. Sometimes, suffering is a necessary part of healing. Q: Your music and influences have clearly evolved over the years, and your latest albums seem to represent a kind of synthesis: a return to the Dark-Electro of your early years combined with the Metal and Industrial influences that followed. How did this evolution come about, and what different stages did you go through to arrive at the final result of “Anatomy Of Suffering”? Kristof: My return to Dark-Electro is not only a response to the demand from the fans, but also a result of all the work I’ve done in the Dark-Ambient world. My love for synthesizers and Eurorack modular systems reignited my passion for Electronic music. While I haven’t completely drifted away from Metal, I’ve become far more selective with it, finding myself increasingly drawn to Electronic and Ambient music instead. Q: Now that Dawn Of Ashes is leaning more towards its Electronic side again, I assume this also impacts your live performances. How is that going these days, and do you notice a different audience or fanbase attending your shows? Kristof: Dawn Of Ashes is now more focused on performing both the older Dark-Electro material and the newer Dark-Electro work. We’re putting live Metal performances on pause for now, as this approach makes touring easier and allows us to focus more fully on the Industrial side of the live experience. Q: A final question that I consider quite important concerns the visual aspect that Dawn Of Ashes has always invested in. I’m thinking, for instance, of the music video for “Viral Decay” from the new album. What are your thoughts and experiences regarding a current zeitgeist in which ‘wokeism’ on the one hand and algorithm-driven censorship culture on the other stand in stark contrast to what you create? Kristof: To be honest, I’ve been much more careful with the visual side of things, as I feel some of the early Dawn Of Ashes themes leaned too heavily into edgelord aesthetics and shock for the sake of shock. Now, everything needs to carry substance and meaning. If the content is controversial, it has to symbolize something deeper—something metaphorical rather than merely provocative.

items.body: Henrik Karlsson might ring a bell for fans of Seven Trees. However, it has been several years since this Swedish project released any new material. In the meantime, one of its members, Henrik Karlsson, began releasing his own music under the sonic alter ego Subverge. Four albums have since been released on his own label, Arcane Dirge. A selection of nine tracks from those albums has been brought together on this compilation, “Select”, and supplemented with three previously unreleased tracks, which also conclude the album. Seven Trees and Subverge are not really comparable, except for their shared Electronic foundations. That said, Subverge appears to draw inspiration from the legacy of Cold Meat Industry. A pronounced Dark-Ambient influence runs throughout the album, although it rapidly evolves into a more Cinematic sound. The result is an overwhelming production built upon an extremely dark undertone, frequently supported by slow rhythms and powerful orchestral percussion. At times, I even detected subtle Tribal elements. Dark strings color the atmosphere, while more delicate piano arrangements provide contrast and depth. Repetitive sequences create a sense of foreboding and further reinforce the album’s gloomy mood. To be fair, I must admit that the three previously unreleased tracks—seemingly older compositions that simply never found their way onto an album—do not add much to the overall experience and therefore offer little real bonus value. Nevertheless, “Select” presents an excellent overview of Subverge’s work and serves as the perfect introduction for newcomers, as well as an ideal opportunity for existing listeners to (re)discover the project. As far as I’m concerned, this is an absolute masterpiece. (Rating:8½). Listen to “Silver Circles”: https://aliensproduction.bandcamp.com/track/silver-circles

items.body: 28 years after the wintry North, BJ Nilsen has released a surprise companion piece as Hazard. That’s a long time, but as one looks back, one gains perspective on earlier works. Winter is approaching in the Southern Hemisphere, which makes the release date fitting for these regions ~ even if these sounds of snow, ice and wind come from the Arctic north. The title, Pre-Lapsarian, refers to the time before the Fall of Humanity, when everything was innocent and pure. Regardless of one’s theology, it’s easy to hear the Arctic soundscape as pristine and undisturbed, even if to human ears it may sound forlorn and abandoned. A soft drone and cold wind launch the recording into the frigid air. Nilsen’s footsteps can be heard amid the quiet rustle, crunching into the snow. Louder sounds in the fourth minute suggest snapping trees and an approaching storm, and as soon as the danger is registered, the pitch of the wind rises. Many artists incorporate field recordings into their music or the other way around, but Nilsen is one of the masters. Allowing the natural sounds to dictate their counterparts, he creates passages that sound entirely organic, even when one knows they are not. Pre-Lapsarian conveys the stark beauty of the Arctic landscape while sculpting a sonic narrative: the distillation of a winter event. When the sound levels subside in the eighth minute, one feels as if one has survived a necessary foray outside one’s shelter and returned just in time. The weather remains frightful, but as the zipper to the tent is re-secured, the field recordist is again safe and sound. (Richard Allen) Available here

items.body: The sharp pluck of a Wayuu classical guitar opens “Cardón” before the bass drops and Afro-Caribbean percussions floods in. Ghetto Kumbé built the track around classical guitarist Henry Pimienta Pushaina and singer Lido Pimienta. Pushaina, a concert musician from Uribia, brings material from his Portafolio de Obras Wayuu para Guitarra, a project that translates ancestral Wayuu melodies to classical guitar. This pairs naturally with Lido Pimienta’s background; born in Barranquilla of mixed Afro-Colombian and Wayuu descent, she blends traditional rhythms like cumbia and bullerengue with synth-pop. Her high, clear vocal cuts straight through the percussion layers. The lyric she wrote with Ghetto Kumbé’s Edgardo Garcés follows someone standing in a river at night, cold water over their feet, their sins going downstream with the current, praying the moon holds the frost back till morning. The chorus keeps returning to “Solo deja que la brisa arrastre todo consigo”, let the breeze carry everything away with it, and Pimienta’s voice delivers it each time like the decision has already been made. Co-produced with London’s The Busy Twist, the Afro-Caribbean percussion drives underneath while the vocal stays above it. “Cardón” opens Cardones, the new Ghetto Kumbé album released on May 15, an eight-track record built around collaborations: Pimienta Pushaina also opens the album on “Wayakana”, while Nidia Gongora and Akilín appear on closing track “Belén”. In support of the LP, the Cardones Tour Europa 2026 runs through June and July, taking in Fusion Festival in Larz, Colours of Ostrava in Ostrava and Les Suds à Arles among the stops.   Stream “Cardón” HERE and get your copy of Cardones following THIS LINK. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — After the revitalization of his solo career by reuniting with Brian Eno, Robert Wyatt, Andy MacKay and Paul Thompson on 6PM in 2004, 50 Minutes Later continued in 2006 with the same team, and it is also called that because as they were recorded in the same recording sessions, it is 50 minutes long, which is the duration of 6PM, then put its continuation.Phil Manzanera had returned and Revolution begins to prove it; Brian Eno's hand is evident in the song, we can imagine Eno singing it, and yet Manzanera plays and the duo works as well as in the 70s, even better, because they sound current, they sound alternative, and if Technicolor UFO can sound like a typical Roxy Music rock, That's All I Know shows us another unequivocally solo facet, where after an acoustic beginning, the sum of instruments will make it esoterically mysterious, enhanced by the chorus as well.50 Minutes Later begins with ambient sound...and although it is not clarified in the credits, the tango that is heard in the background, as if playing in the middle of the street, is sung by Adriana Varela, an Argentine singer and this inclusion is not accidental, because later the theme will develop a kind of suggested electronic tango, which will never end up exploding, it is the atmosphere that floats, its spirit, with included recitation, the piano and the cornet of Robert Wyat are so jazzy that they end up being tango, because both are urban genres born around the same time and that at times touch each other.Desparecido continues the tango flirtation, sung half in English, half in Spanish, with guitar work that perfectly understands the provocative, streetwise nature of the genre, I know this because I know tango and I've liked it for a long time, and at the same time fuses it with something more rock-oriented and contemporary. But tango allows for many fusions, ever since the 70s, and just as Kurt Weill fused opera with cabaret, this tango with alternative rock and Floydian airs flows naturally, especially because Manzanera knew what he was getting into.The tracks are linked, like a suite within the album. You can hear a train, and Dusza with his folkloric percussion, also related to the fusion that Fernando Samalea (Charly Garc�a's drummer) has been doing on his solo albums for years, until "One Step" returns with the sharp electric guitar, traversing a nighttime street illuminated by car headlights, painting it like a rainbow shimmering in the humidity.A drum'n'bass track with guitar and chorus sounds as current as the entire proposed fusion, a step further, daring not to stagnate their vision. The guitar changes tones during the same long and sinuous solo, shifting from rock and ambient...to distorted jazz, until "Swimming," which wouldn't be out of place on Brian Eno's Before and After Scene, glides serenely with melodies that seem to belong to another world, which is definitely what Bible Black would do, making us not miss the 70s, because by turning the right way, everything is in the present; that's what the cover logo is about. Till the End of the Line with just a double bass creating an atmosphere almost like John Cale's, and that's what the song is about in its cosmic country rock, how the extremes are touched at the end...that ending with a heartbreaking, emotional and clarifying guitar solo.This comeback not only features furious guitars, but also atmospheres, sensations, and suggestions to be taken and expanded upon, making the album interactive, with subtle moods, melodies...as well as "no man's land," virgin territory to claim, call it psychedelia, Canterbury Scene, call it part of Phil Manzanera's return to the most elaborated rock scene.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — It's always a fine green morning (wink, nod) in ProgRogue Land when I get a message from Ally Carter, with a nice download for me to peruse. Because it invariably means a new album is about to be released from this talented band that I happen to admire since their debut. Their seventh album is the second volume of last year's tasty The Land, the Sea, the Air, which garnered rave reviews from yours truly as pretty much the majority of the Prog community. Ally, Tree, David and Tom are back once again, as if it was only yesterday , consolidating their musical stance on the degrading ecology of our tired planet. At the risk of repeating myself, this band sticks to its principles with orthodox zeal, maintaining not only their style and their immediately recognizable sound, but also keeping continuity with a personal artwork display that is applause worthy. Three mega tracks are their usual recipe, and why change that, after all they are not the Ramones! "Song of the Rainforest" will dominate 21 minutes and 21 seconds of your time, keeping you far away from those pesky cell phones, as well as all other modern technological distractions. Tree Stewart settles the proper mood on her perennially silky keyboards, stitching into the melodic fabric a sundry of effects, bassist Dave Greenaway laying down his basso profundo with meticulous authority, Tom Jackson ticking, tocking and otherwise locking, straight into the groove. Ally glides in with his jade green guitar unbothered , caressing his neck with one hand , while the other performs various wrist flickers on his six strings. The atmosphere is set, perhaps somewhere deep in the Colombian forest where it rains more than anywhere else, an ode to the mighty power that Mother Nature chooses to unleash willy nilly, at her discretion. When Ally interjects with his brassy saxophone, the instrument most resembling the human voice, he pleads the case for all mankind. When the blowing gets severe, it's surely a sign of repentance and begging for forgiveness. Heavy weather jazz time. The sweeping keyboards convey the sorrowful resignation of endless human intrusion into where it shouldn't belong, her ominously angry synthesizers (and famed Roli Seaboard) slash fiercely in defence of the despairing jungle and its right to survive, I daresay even flourish. Still heavy but not quite jazzy, more like organized bedlam. And then, extended peaceful interjections of velvety softness come across as soothing panacea, Tree's flutes leading the serene parade, ethereal yet very much alive. The crushing solemnity in the final section is heart stopping, Tree and Ally laying down a magic carpet ride of contemplative introspection, maybe even self healing, in essence. When the rhythm section forcefully slams its foot down, it serves as a defensive anchor being cast, a line in the forest that will not be invaded anymore, come hell or (gulp) high water! In my mind, and assuredly yours when you hear it, this is their finest track and finest hour ever. There is a reason why Tree Stewart was voted among the top keyboard players in prog recently, she can play like the wind, as witnessed by her immaculate display on piano on "Rivers of Tears", mastering not only technique but also impeccable emotion, as one can hear the rivers and the tears in her performance. Throw in the lush orchestrations, Ally's discreet guitar tremors, the subtle cymbal work, and the reverence in the bass, the only discovery left is Tree's vocal which is delivered with empathy. The swerve into a jazzier surroundings becomes obvious as the piano and sax conspire to whip up some well-deserved groovy frenzy, after all, these are consummate musicians! This 15-minute epic refuses to stick too long in any redundancy, so the mid-section suddenly flips the script by injecting more sombre sequences, led by a forcefully darker vocal chant, and then plummeting into complex rhythmic polyrhythmic chaos that will drop that jaw of yours. The churning keyboards swirl and twirl like dervishes on fire. Tree even daring a few 'space shanties' made famous by the late Gilly Smith of Gong. This section surely owes some winks toward that legendary band; there are many little hints one can discern. And just when you may think 'what could they possibly come up with next after such a two-handed slap across the musical face', the band opt for a swooning melody so immediately attractive that I fell to my knees hearing the first time, sung with utter conviction, as a cross between Olivia Sparnenn of Mostly Autumn and hint of Janis Joplin, I swear on my honour! Here, total simplicity rules, the orchestral keyboards convey harmony only a song title called "Paradise" could get away with. Indeed, this is most heavenly, even the sax plays the gentle card. Nearly 9 minutes of bliss that could have/should have/and would have continued for another 10 minutes, making my day and night. Wow! Their best yet. 5 seasons of Green

items.body: Review by Aussie-Byrd-Brother — Always a recurring home for titles and artists on the darker end of the Italian prog spectrum, Black Widow Records brings together theatrical doom metal band ExpiatoriA and established gothic/symphonic/dark RPI group Il Segno del Comando for a glum and evocative split album `Voci Notturne', inspired by an Italian TV series from 1995 of the same name. Working alongside each-other, the two acts have set out to recreate, in their own unique and individual styles, the eerie, cryptic and perplexing atmosphere of the show, and listeners essentially receive an EP's worth of new music from each of them.An aura of intrigue hovers over director Pupi Avati's broadcast and the subsequent distribution of the TV series `Voci Notturne' ("Nocturnal Voices" in English), considered a masterpiece of darkness and mystery. The ambiguous narrative weaves together politics, religion, history and the supernatural across continents and decades, with an unsettling atmosphere that grows as truth and illusion blur together. The fact that the series is not readily accessible in the modern era (outside of a heavily reworked and reedited version) has only enhanced its allure and reputation.Formed in Genoa in 1987, ExpiatoriA only released their debut album `Shadows' in 2022, with a live cassette following two years later. Taking the opening side here, the band offers a set of three murky doom metal dirges of branching passages and moods. Front and centre are vocalist AngeleX's pained vocals, moving between despairing wailing and slurred, guttural growling, and they envelope the band's sludgy riffing, mud-thick fuzzy bass rumbles and battering-ram drums with a suffocating and disorientating fervour. Spectral choirs, ghostly church organ and spoken word passages intensify the sombre ambience, but there are fleeting little glimpses of light and grandiosity.The flip-side comes from Il Segno del Comando, with over 30 years of standout modern dark RPI and gothic rock works to their name. Over the years, the group has constantly refined and altered their approach, moving between heavy underground rock and more overtly progressive rock arrangements (lots of vigorous and upfront keyboard soloing these days!). In contrast to ExpiatoriA's interpretations, ...Comando's pieces are more up-tempo, punchier and rockier, with many bombastic and stirring moments.Riccardo Morello's soulful commanding croon purrs throughout `Le due vie', where reflective reaching guitar strains kick in with a strident power, and no shortage of wavering Moog trills and glistening synths. `Il crittogramma' thrums with slinking electronics and runaway guitar-soloing, and `Litania per Emily e Giacomo' is a rousing and sophisticated ballad with elegant orchestration, making it the most overtly melodic moment of the album (a track that would actually be welcome on any RPI album). Closer `Egregoro' is a tasty instrumental of heavy guitars and plentiful synth soloing, contrasting reflective passages with ballsy hard-rock crunch, not unlike UK band Arena in parts. Infectious and addictive, what a powerful and memorable way to close the LP!Available on LP, CD and downloads, if you're one of those drawn to the shadowy corners occupied by darker Italian prog and unconventional metal acts, `Voci Notturne' just might be the temptation you need to fall for.Three and a half stars, rounded up to four for the Archives.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'A Dramatic Turn of Events' is the eleventh full-length studio album from Dream Theater and theirfirst with then-new drummer Mike Mangini, who filled the spot for the leaving Mike Portnoy. To myunderstanding, the majority of the drum parts for this album had actually been written prior to thearrival of Mangini, and therefore, he does not get any songwriting credits. Nevertheless, thisrecord delivers the familiar sound of Dream Theater in spades, and despite a few moments ofexperimentation or play-around with other styles, many would safely call this a typical DT release.Compositionally, this is one of the strongest and most sophisticated works from the band, with themajority of the songs being rather lengthy, whereas the album itself bolsters a running time ofseventy-seven-plus minutes, which is a certain prerequisite for a demanding listen. I personallyenjoy this album every time I play it - the riffs sound really refreshing and the unbridledcomplexity of the instrumental sections genuinely blows my head off in a way that only Dream Theaterare able to achieve.Kicking off in a typical melodramatic fashion, we have the excellent song 'On the Backs of Angels',which sees Jordan Rudess playing a continuum in the intro section, and John Petrucci laying down oneof the most effective solos on the album. Apart from this, this song is by far one of the most"typical" Dream Theater compositions on here, which is definitely not a drawback, having become oneof their most well-known songs in recent years. Next up is 'Build Me Up, Break Me Down', a shortersong that instead tries to break away from the band's usual sound and introduces a crunchy nu-metalaesthetic, which is pretty interesting (given that the end result is really solid). The third albumtrack 'Lost Not Forgotten' is an intense piece of prog metal containing all the delightfully complextwists and turns one would expect from Rudess and Petrucci's writing, who would establish themselvesas the primary songwriters of the band for years to come. More melodic guitars enter the scene onthe following track 'This Is the Life', which among other things, slows down the album after thebombastic beginning. With the synth-laden prog rollercoaster 'Bridges in the Sky' and the anthemicsuite 'Outcry', Dream Theater mark a return to their epic sound, offering two lengthy songs thatimpress with some truly creative sections, very musical and ornately composed. The final tracks onthis record include the elegiac 'Far from Heaven', the theatrical epic 'Breaking All Illusions' anda decent pop song that closes off ADTOE.This album does not redefine the progressive metal genre, but in my view this was never the point ofit. It simply serves as an excellent example of songwriting mastery and in my ears happens to be oneof Dream Theater's most consistent efforts in the last fifteen years or so.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Having been listening to this album for years now, I still find the opening track 'The City Has NoEmpathy' the most interesting and memorable part of it. 'Scenes from Ephemeral City' is the 2011self-released debut studio album from Australian progressive rock/metal band Caligula's Horse, whowere founded by guitarist Sam Vallen (who is the engineer and producer of this release) and vocalistJim Grey sometime in 2010. The band's powerful and melodic style is quite impressive and immediate,as heard on this daring debut collection, which is also fairly accessible. Achieving a fine balancebetween the technical guitar-heavy parts and the dreamier melodic passages, C-Horse deliver arecognizable style that definitely emphasizes the warm and expressive singing style of Jim Grey, whois a truly excellent performer. 'Scenes' was definitely composed by guitar player Sam Vallen, whoexhibits a fabulous command of his instrument, including several crafty acoustic bits, a good amountof really technical, proggy riffs, and an abundance of musically acute solos.The music on this album resembles the output of Scale the Summit, Plini and Haken, all of which arecontemporaries of Caligula's Horse, and are often mentioned together in discussions on the new waveof prog metal. As for the album itself, the original track list features seven songs, of which theaforementioned opening track is a really strong contender for being one of the most memorable piecesof modern prog metal, with its gritty guitar playing and inviting vocals. The two instrumentals'Singularity' and 'Calliope's Son' are really good, too, but some of the longer tracks like 'Alonein the World' (sitting at eleven minutes) and 'Silence' (at seven) fail to leave a lastingimpression and miss that characteristic sound or hook that the band would deliver on subsequentreleases. The Inside Out Music reissue of this LP features two extra tracks, of which the single'Colossus' is a really fine entry and once again exhibits the inherent melodicism within Caligula'sHorse's songwriting. Overall, this is an impressive debut album, especially given the fact that itwas self-produced and self-released (it does sound great all the way through!), but it lacks notableideas, which makes it one of the least impressive corners of the band's discography.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — "Gil Gilad was formed in County Durham, UK, in 1979 by university students interested in long-form music. The original members went their separate ways sometime after 1981. Three of the original members (Paul Dobson, Kev Stevens, and Nev Tobin) started writing music again starting around 2015 when the band made its appearance with a Facebook page sharing tracks from Soundcloud. After many years, the band finally released its debut album in 2024 titled 'A Record of the Unworldly and the Strange' inspired by entrepreneur and chemist John Walker. The current line-up as of December 2025 is Paul Dobson (guitars, keyboards, backing vocals), Nev Tobin (lead vocals, keyboards), Kev Stevens (drums, keyboards, guitar, backing vocals), and Geoff Parkin (lead guitar, backing vocals)". This is the second chapter in the Walker saga, and as such, the band take us on a sweeping 70-minute sonic adventure, with nods and winks to a series of classic British writers as well as harkening back at classics like Jeff Wayne's War of the Worlds.HG Wells is the ignition for the opener "Prisoners of Time", a prototypical neo-prog track that features all the instrumentalists showing off their wares, blitzing synthesizer and keyboard runs, solid bass underfoot, concrete drum propellants and Nev Tobin's rather attractive vocal tone and delivery. 'We all have time machines?those that take us back are memories and those that carry us forward are dreams.'Up next under the auspices of philosopher, logician, mathematician Bertrand Russell "We Are Scientists Not Philosophers" selects a lighter approach to complex thought based on 'Science is what you know. Philosophy is what you don't know'. Here the tempo is first leisurely and playful, with a sudden plunge into darker spheres where the austere narration challenges the weakness of mind. The rhythmic piano is maddeningly efficient, as it sits front and center, its ivory keys glowing brightly. There is a definite art-rock slant, perhaps winking at bands like 10cc or even Alan Parsons Project. "The Traveller: Altered Destiny" has theoretical physicist Charles Peacock as an influence, and musically, the APP hint comes across luminously, swirling keyboard setting the foundation on which basic bass and drum stakes are planted 'We explore the vagaries of time; Parallel worlds where everything happens in tandem with everything else. However, our minds are ill-disposed to extract the truth behind the thin veils that blind us.' An exuberant electronic prog workout that offers a most attractive plane to enjoy, melodically powerful, yet accessible, full of thrilling spills. There is an 80s electro feel to the vocals which are extremely attractive, as it comes across well with all the backing mellotrons, a fascinating track to be sure! John Walker speaking of his loss of Hai-Yun is expressed on "A Chance to Speak" , a short two-minute waver, dispensing a very elegant British sound, focused on piano and aery vocals. 'I last saw her on the outskirts of Durham?How she danced on those silken, silver threads I will never know: She was elegance and strength, and light as floating feathers?'. A proggier trio of tracks form the middle core of this release, and my favourite section , first up "The Watchers", owner of a cinematic slice of imaginary sights and sounds, caught in a lush whirlwind, immediately attractive with a strong melodic spine and dramatic vocals that include amazing, hushed backing vocals and effects galore. 'The primary objective of a Watcher is to ensure the safety and security of the community, by whatever means necessary within the limits of the primary directive set out in Principles of Service'. This track could have ben a segue to APP's I Robot masterpiece "The Voice". Next of kin, "Escape from York" possesses a cosmic urgency that felt like running from the devil. Hurried, panting and awesome electronics make this cascading piece of energy most compelling. The looping bass finale a killer. 'We need to go, or you will not live out the hour!' . Who else but the perennial JRR Tolkien as inspiration on a Kate Bush-like vocal to die for on "A Walk in the Woods" (6:14), a stylistically dynamic tour de force, showing intense attention to mood and atmosphere, a comfortable sense of freedom of pace, even though engulfed in the mysterious solitude of nature. 'I thought all the trees were whispering to each other, passing news and plots along in an unintelligible language; and the branches swayed and groped without any wind.' The loving screech of Geoff Parkin's electric guitar does the piece justice. A definite highlight. A welcome return to "Dreams of Samira" channels a page from Percy Byshe Shelley's Love's Philosophy, recalling German band RPWL in terms of style and structure, keyboard and rhythm section heavy, sliced open by a bitter guitar recollection, weaving expertly with a companion synthesizer expression, piano and mellotron to finish off. 'Nothing in the world is single, All things by a law divine. In one spirit meet and mingle. Why not I with thine?'On the two next thrilling pieces, William Gibson the American-Canadian writer ("Neuromancer") provides the essence for the more experimental "The Burghers", a clanging glance into the impending fate of mankind, based on sociological conflicts that are now a global spectacle. Cyberpunk rebellion of yore now transforming itself into internet anarchy. 'The future has already arrived; it's just not evenly distributed yet'. Musically, it's a deliberate ball of confusing distortions, oblique settings and a desperately gloomy finale. "Before Today is Yesterday" suggests too many voices in our heads, forming a dangerously growing series of phenomena as insomnia, depression and data fatigue. No time left for yesterday's reality, only tomorrow's incertitude. Opinion-peddling rules the day. 'And we danced on the brink of an unknown future, to an echo from a vanished past'. Nev Tobin stars on the grim "Darkened Embers of Suspicion" has a slight Kashmir-ian aura (the Led Zep version , not the disputed region!), a brooding snarl of reflection, the result of the previous discussed tracks, focusing on endless negatives, eschewing whatever progressive good has been achieved on so many levels. Negativity sells. 'In the wastelands of memory, our past haunts us when all is dark and rested. We become robed in lost moments, and half remembered phrases that twist and torment'.The pleasantly lilting "The Strange Long Night" hides an underlying message of disbelief 'Believe what? That tomorrow night beneath the full moon, I'll sprout hair and fangs and eat people? It's bulls**t!'. The piece is somewhat dark, quirky and oblique, the way an odd lengthy evening may easily become. What better segue than the tempestuous fury of "The Storm", a six-minute+ tornado of sound with raging synths, howling gales of mellotron, booming bass curvatures and tectonic drum patterns that will stimulate the blood flow. 'Batten down and lock up! Sound the alarm! Storm coming!'. A relentless pummeling can do wonders for the energy levels, lest we forget that Mother Nature can be cruel to be kind, in the right measure. The 70-minute opus finalizes its run on "The Nature of Time", a hint from William Wordsworth's "Composed During a Storm", showing abundantly the painstaking details marshaled by the band in maintaining flow, thematically as well as infusing sufficient musical variety to keep the headphones on, all along the adventure. "He raised his eye Soul-smitten; for, that instant, did appear large space ('mid dreadful clouds) of purest sky, An azure disc, shield of Tranquillity; Invisible, unlooked-for, minister of providential goodness ever nigh!". A solitary two-note piano puts this to bed effortlessly.An excellent album, that caught me quite by surprise, as the first audition had not grabbed me completely. By the second, it was hook, line and sinker. Bravo, lads , well played! 4.5 whiskey sours.

items.body: Review by Finnforest — Another Mystifying Turn While 1989 saw the release of the wonderful archival Donna Plautilla, it also brought asecond release that year in the form of Non Mettere Le Dita Nel Naso. Google translates thisto "Don't Put Your Fingers in Your Nose," which sums up pretty well, unintentionally or perhapssubconsciously, how unnecessary this release actually was. Confusing labeling indicates both a Bancoalbum and a Francesco Di Giacomo solo album, almost as if the PR team involved couldn't figure outwhat it really was. After hearing the music, one can understand why.I will give them credit for keeping the songwriting in house. Other established pop/rock artistsbegan subbing out this most important part of their craft to paid "hitmakers." While that practicehad always happened for non-songwriter "performers," it is tragic when it becomes embraced by actualmusicians who have proven their songwriting skills already in the past, only to capitulate theirpersonal artistry to product movers due either to label pressure or lost artist confidence. The material here is sadly reminiscent to E Via, though not identical. It has perhaps morerange of styles, better arrangements, and just slightly longer tracks for elaboration. As always,the Banco musicians and the long roster of guests are fantastic players, and we are treated totalent and production quality that stands with anyone. However, as with E Via, the problem isthe material. Who are they making this record for? Despite the treasure they have in Di Giacomo'svoice, despite the finesse of all players involved, there is nothing here that is going to excitethe progressive rock fans of the Darwin era. There is nothing that excites me as a fan ofBuone Notizie's surprisingly fun concoction of mischief and chops. It has a few interesting performance and sound choices here and there. "Qualcosa che rimane" is thestandout moment showcasing Francesco in the spotlight with only very subtle and refined keyboardsand guitar as support. But even if the goal here was pop perfection, others do it better. Thesetracks are a bit long-winded and middle-of-the-road to capture the succinct sugar high pop fanscrave. What to even compare this to? Mid '80s Meatloaf, Celine Dion, a lesser Steve Winwood moment?Answer: It doesn't matter. The only thought I have while listening is pondering what else I could belistening to instead. There is a templated contrivance to the song structures which stranglesimmediacy---very "session-y" sounding instrumental leads laid atop an almost programmed-feeling,often generic backing.The music is not necessarily bad if you have a fetish for sophisticated, middle-aged empty-caloriegloss, and I again resist giving Banco the one-star treatment out of respect for these legendary RPImusicians. But I just can't recommend this album enthusiastically to anyone either. It doesn'tconnect with me in any way. It feels lost in terms of finding its own niche or even finding its ownnecessity. The apparent lack of direction at this point would be further evidenced two years laterwhen they would remake their first two classic albums. I can't get excited about that either. I haveno interest in hearing progressive rock icons attempt to re-conjure the magic of glorious youth,whether that is Banco or Roger Waters. So in my eyes, it does feel like Banco is now firmly lost inthe wilderness artistically. All that said, I also worry this overly harsh take may stem from my own myopic taste profiles, and Iadmit to being less certain about the rating than I was with E Via. Thus I hope others herewill double check me on this---listen to this album and review it. Am I missing the genius somehow?

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — An utterly unique band to emerge in Spain's late 70s prog scene, AZAHAR which was named after anorange blossom flower and really did bloom into its own unique cultivar of musical ingenuity thatcould be referred to as something like symphonic progressive space Rock Andaluz. This band was oneof the first progressive bands to emerge in 1976 after the collapse of the Franco regime anddelivered two extraordinary albums in its three year run before exiting the scene in 1979. Despiteits short run the band had a significantly different lineup on its two albums with only vocalistDick Zappala and guitarist Antonio Valls appearing on the two releases. On this debut ELIXIR whichcame out in 1977, keyboardist Gusatovo Ros and bassist Jorge Barrai filled the remaining slots.AZAHAR was a very rare breed in that it managed to release an entire album with no drummer to befound which is practically unheard of in any sort of rock music. Instead the primary rhythmicbackbone was delivered by the thumping bass grooves. An elegant album that featured seven distinct track that didn't quite reach the 38 minute mark,ELIXIR featured extremely lush and complex keyboard arrangements accompanied by catchy flamencoinfused melodies along with passionate vocals as well as driving rock guitar heft and heavy bassgrooves sounding something like an oddball mix of Triana, the French space rock act Pulsar, thepastoral folky aspects of Genesis along with knotty prog time signature workouts and unexpectedtransitions. Add to that beautiful Middle Eastern melodic touches all completely forged without theaid of a drummer. The extra emphasis is clearly on the rich layers of synthesizers, Fender Rhodesand mellotrons but the flamenco and rock guitar parts are very much in the forefront much of thetime as well. Very much in vein of the Rock Urbano that was underway, AZAHAR delivered passionateSpanish lyrics emulating the style of the Italian prog scene however the Andalusian flamenco kept itfirmly on Spanish territory.The opening "Campos de Azahar" ushers in the album with larger than life layers of keyboard swellswhich sets the tone for the space rock aspects of the album and it's not until well into the secondtrack "�Qu� malo hay, se�or juez?" that the rock guitar kicks in and then game on as the bandengages in one of those dialogue albums where the keys and guitar parts sound like their talking toeach other. The third track "�Es que esto no tiene nombre!" introduces a greater emphasis on moreangular progressive complexities time signatures run amok, hairpin turns into varying motifs and amost satisfying scorching acid rock soloing sequence that trades off with the keys in unique ways.In some ways it reminds me of what Symphony X would latch onto a couple decades down the road onlythis track is more like the ridiculously extreme crafty complex antics of bands like the ArgentineanAlas or Italian masters Museo Rosenbach. Some of the keyboards remind me of the French zeuhl actArcha�a when sustained oscillating high notes roar above it all.The balance between instrumental development and vocal led structured songs give the album abeautifully eclectic style as well as the dynamics shifting from more pastoral sensual folky motifsand then into crescendoing uproars of keys and guitars getting wild. Vocal aspects are diverse aswell with not only passionately delivered lyrics out of the Italian prog playbook but also findmoments of group harmonies. Extra touches from the mandolin and Middle Eastern rhythms weaved intothe flamenco and symphonic prog is beautifully performed. Other tracks such as "Mercaderes," "UnHombre Cansado" and "Cantaros de Fuego" continue the magic with the latter offering some of thecoolest bass lines in prog but the highlight may be the closing three part suit "Viaja a Marruecos"which wastes no time delivering the prog goods with an endless parade of variations throughsymphonic prog turf alternating with Spanish folk featuring Zappala's fluid vocal style. While nodrummer is one board a bit of exotic percussion actually finds its way onto this track offering someof the best excursions into Middle Eastern sounds. The band delivers on all pistons offering thisamazing climactic closer that ends in with a frenzied cyclical loop that ends the prog party well.I guess i'm on the opposite spin of most regarding this album considering how low its generallyrated but for my tastes this is one of my absolute favorite prog albums of the entire Spanish sceneand as far as Rock Andaluz bands go this band does it for me much more than Triana and other actsdue to the fact that this band had a creative edge unlike any other in Spain or anywhere for thatmatter. This album stands out as an utterly unique example of prog ingenuity nurtured in every waydelivering top notch melodies, brilliant arrangements and an even more impressive execution of itall. This album IMHO imbues the very essence of what Spanish prog was all about in the late 1970ssounding like all of the bands of the era rolled into one with the exception the jazz fusionists asthis album does not delve into jazz fueled frenzies however some of the most sophisticated progmoves do match that level of ingenuity. This is literally one of those albums i can listen torepeatedly and never tired of. Masterpiece in my book.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — After a very eclectic debut that eschewed the typical Rock Andaluz playbook that was rockin' Spainin the latter half of the 1970s, the Madrid act AZAHAR followed "Elixir" two years later with itssecond album simply with an eponymous title and refined its sound to a more mainstream stylecourtesy of the addition of drummer Willy Rodriguez de Trujillo who hailed from Seville and honedhis chops with local bands such as Fly, Blizzard and Manantial. He replaced bassist Jorge Barral andsurprisingly the band didn't employ a new bassist for the part but rather used two sessionmusicians: Julio Blasco and Enrique Carmona to fill his shoes. Likewise keyboardist Gusatovo Ros(who left to form Azabache) was replaced by the less flamboyant Manolo Manrique so when the dustsettled it was really only vocalist Dick Zappala and guitarist Antonio Valls returning with acompletely different set of musicians around them.It's immediately apparent on the opening track "Expresso a Ketama" that the band shifted gearssignificantly by adopting the standard Rock Andaluz format of guitar, bass, keys and drums with thefocus on the flamenco rhythms in a standard rock format and deemphasizing the keys that were sodominant on the debut to more of an accent piece with piano runs, and more symphonic light elements.In this regard the band emulated the more pop infused bands such as Alameda or Triana, in a waysounding like something in between the two. While the debut fearlessly treaded in highly progressiveterrain, this second offering plays it safe which was usually the case with the late to the progparty Spanish scene with bands sowing their prog oats on the debut and then forced by financiallimitations to simplify their approach.The second track "La Naranja y el Lim�n" continues the simplified style and was released as a singleshowcasing the band's ability to craft beautiful flamenco infused pop hooks like the best of theSpanish bands. The album pretty much sticks to the new sanctified playbook alternating betweensomewhat faster paced tracks including the instrumental "Zahira" and the slower tracks with thelengthiest track "El Mago Acidote" serving as the best example at 9 1/2 minutes in playing time witha slow ballad-like demeanor yet salvaged by Zappala's passionate vocal delivery which showcases hisrange and creative singing style. The track "Aire y Fuego" offers some interesting syncopationoddities while retaining its flamenco rock sensibilities along with some of the Middle Easternflavors from the debut. The closing "Espresso de Ketama" closes with a another flamenco flavoredinstrumental with a bit more emphasis on the keyboards.Overall this is a major departure from the uninhibited creativity of the debut which for my tastesyielded one of the best progressive rock albums in all of Spain. This self-titled followup is muchmore streamlined for the marketplace and features a fairly uniform approach rather than theexcessive extravaganza of "Elixir." While i much prefer the crafty compositions of the debut, for amore commercial approach, AZAHAR did a really great job of suppressing their most uninhibited progartistry and kept in on the leash while fortifying their standard approach with many of the sameflavors only used more as accent sounds rather than the whole enchilada. While the debut ranks highin my world, this second album is still decent although in this more mainstream style i'd preferTriana, Alameda or even the super slick pop rock band Asfalto nevertheless this is a reallyenjoyable album when taking it at face value and leaving comparisons to the debut behind. This wasthe end of the road for AZAHAR despite 1979 being the peak year of prog releases emerging in Spain.
