items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the most important underground innovators of the psychedelic years in the former Soviet Unionwas the Crimean born YURI MOROZOV (later settling in St Petersburg) who was a multidisciplinarymulti-instrumentalist, sound engineer and prolific composer having released well over 50 albums thattackled virtually every modern genre of the era. Completely banned by the Soviet authorities anddenied access to the state label Melodiya, MOROZOV took matters into his own hands by releasing hismusic through the clandestine "samizdat" tape-trading networks which of course were totally illegalbut provided the means for experimental artists who dabbled out of the confines of the strict Sovietcensorship to release their music to the greater public at large.While the USSR was way behind the curve as far as Western musical innovations were concerned,bootlegs still infiltrated beyond the Iron Curtain and influences were adopted. What was really rarethough was for an artist to successfully record in such abundance and release dozens of recordingsto the public all without the sanctity of the state. MOROZOV was not only one of the most prolificand successful of these artists but one of the most wildly experimental. In fact i've never heardanything from USSR that matches his wild excursions into total psychedelic escapism as MOROZOV's 70sreleases with this one, "Сон в красном тереме (Dream of the Red Chamber)" sitting as one of the mostuninhibited albums of all to emerge from the former USSR.This renowned tape recording that finally found a vinyl release in 2014 was recorded between 1973and 1976 although the official date by some is 1975. Apparently the original release featured lesstracks than the 2014 reissue and like all Soviet artifacts from the past, especially from the deepunderground remains a little murky in details but one thing is for sure and that is the fact MOROZOVtruly captured the spirit of the psychedelic 60s and took it all the way to the level of the mostkosmische trip out musical statements of the German Krautrock scene. This album is based on aconcept adopted from the Chinese novel called "Dream Of The Red Chamber" but the musical flow ismore akin to a psychological mind trip taking the most lysergic aspects of psychedelic rock to theirmost terrifying limits. MOROZOV was a master of overdubbing and sound manipulation, sort of theAchim Reichel of the USSR only with a bit of Daevid Allen's Gong thrown in for good measure.The album original featured two versions of the title track broken down into two parts. Highlyexperimental in nature, the music features psychedelic rock, Russian folk, progressive rock and lotsof the earliest examples of the Soviet electronic music scene. It's a shape shifting type of albumthat goes for the psychedelic jugular. Many will find this aimless and simply self-indulgent as it'sa really difficult album to follow. Is there any point to it at all? Well, who knows. It sounds veryimprovisational with little to latch onto as far as structured compositions are concerned howeverit's psychedelic after all and if the aim of the genre is to create an ethereal otherworldly effectwhere the status quo is blissfully ignored and replaced by a consciousness recalibration sessionthen this is indeed the ticket especially considering the time and place of its creation. It's verymuch a dream state kind of album and in that regard it's brilliant. While the musical motifs are very non-musical there are plenty of avant-garde excursions thatimplement patterns of some sort. It's like listening to alien music in that regard. MOROZOV hasoften been called the Soviet version of Sun Ra and that would be quite fitting indeed as thisrelease is very much like Sun Ra's most "out there" moments even if it's not rooted in jazz.Obviously not to everyone's tastes but for the moments when i really want to take a deep dive intoextremely surreal soundscapes and simple psych flavored pop just won't cut it, albums like this riseto the top of the ranks and for my liking this is pure genius in how it exemplifies the spectrum ofthe most underground sounds compiled into a menagerie of free form psychedelic through the 65 minuteplaying time that is available for sampling (forget finding a real copy!) A true underground Sovietclassic here!4.5 rounded down

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Dutch composer and multi-instrumentalist Ruud Dielen unleashes another thrilling album, progressing now into the upper echelons of quality prog, as this is a standout release that had me smiling all the way through. Ably assisted in the task, bassist Tim Ros and drummer Kike Paglia man the rhythm section with authority, introducing three vocalists into the process, Frank van der Borg and Jyoti Verhoeff on lead and backing while Ties van Diesen on backing duties. Harrie Knapen adds Hammond and piano, Thomas Zunk with theremin and mellotron and sax player Reg Parham completing the line-up. The progression is obvious from the first note, as the album unleashes a snarling five-part title track opus that revs on all cylinders like a well-oiled machine. All the ingredients are in place, from an extended electronic introduction that seems to float above the clouds , settling the sonic groundwork into a comfortable zone. The mighty mellotron shows its impeccable grandeur in creating the symphonic mood that it manages so well. On "Part 2: Carrying the Yoke", the arrangement opens up the throttle in a more conventional neo-prog setting, laden with sharper tones, coarse guitar interventions and bombastic keyboard sweeps that elevate the vocals, at times gentle and then more forceful. Veering into more fleecier realms, where ethereal vocalizations (Jyoti) rule the heavens, "Part 3: Into the Clouds" showcases Ruud playing a rolling fretless undertow that hits the mark, thumping drum attack, as the tempo increases into a fiery hurricane of interweaving sounds. The splendid lead guitar work portrays a diversity that oozes class. Another brief instrumental bridge only adds even more pace and drama to the entire opus, setting the stage for another swift turn into the unexpected. "Part 5: Chaotic Spell" swerves into more intricate signatures, a demanding almost Zappa-esque escapade with bold jazz-rock tendencies, a platform for some delirious saxophone ramblings (Parham) and lead guitar forays that exude utter confidence. The drums flutter with a maddening splurge that defies the norms, propelling this finale with resolved expertise. Well done! "If You Please" is an extended instrumental rocker, an opportunity for Ruud to exploit his talents on electric guitar, using a wide variety of tonal shifts, assorted pedals (including the much-beloved wah-wah pedal). At times, it felt like Hillage-era Gong mixed in with ZZ Top zaniness, perfectly egged on by a dynamic rhythmic engine. Well-dressed fish ! Brooding strings, a hint of theremin, distant organ and mellotron on "If I Only", setting the table for an ominously sombre vocal 'devoid of empathy', both pleading their case with measured conviction. The biting guitar snarl heightening the theatrics, both rhythm shavings and lead flickers, the manic percussive attitude pervasive and threatening. Another excellent slice of prog rock. Keeping the thrill vibrant, the tentacular keyboard display on "Whirlwinds & Maelstroms" does the trick, a piece where the mellotrons blaze, the extended Hammond organ eventually overtaking the mood with a thorough onslaught of gloomy thunder, enough room left for the acerbic guitar shards to cut hard and deep into the flesh. These boys know how to play. Masterclass effort. The finale "Everything Must Break to Grow- Part 2 Reprise" surprises once again, as the female vocals (Jyoti and Ties) take over rather brilliantly in a vaporous premise, with huge harmony backing vocals, a dreamy soundscape floating in psychedelic karma. This turns into a rockier variation that shows plenty of backbone, as if the Legendary Pink Dots were the reference point, mostly evident on the voice effected final section with hallucinogenic tendencies that cannot be overlooked. Effing splendid, if I say so myself! The entire project did not need to rely on any 'elements of hope' to succeed but rather was dependant on raw unadulterated talent, cohesion, inspiration and dedication to create interesting musical statements. The Glorious Wolf has truly arrived.4.5 Cosmic hunters

items.body: Starsign emerged in the 1990s and was driven by the German duo Oliver Teßmer and Matthias Blechschmidt. At the time, they released several EPs, along with an album that appeared in 2003. After that, things went quiet for more than two decades, but the duo revived the project a few years ago. Following several high-profile singles, they released “Silver Linings” earlier this year, featuring 10 tracks. The influences running through “Silver Linings” are quite diverse, yet they fit perfectly within the Electro-Pop genre. The songs move between quiet, floating pieces on the one hand and more danceable tracks on the other. Depeche Mode can occasionally be felt lurking around the corner, while other tracks seem inspired by Mesh. However, Starsign is by no means a copycat; rather, they have managed to blend these diverse elements into a smooth and enjoyable whole. Some songs are beautifully crafted and reveal subtle details in the production. Personally, I prefer their ‘heavier’ tracks, and although I do miss an undeniable standout hit on the album, “Silver Linings” still has a great deal to offer. (Rating:8). items.body: The new single S + M from Staytus has the crackling charge of a bad idea unraveling like a ball of blood red yarn. Sam Grundemann, the Los Angeles artist behind Staytus, has built the project around industrial pressure, electronic gloss, horror-film glamour, and the private emotional mess that keeps people returning to situations they swore they had outgrown. With her new single and video, released following her signing to Cleopatra Records, she turns separation, obsession, and the pull of reconciliation into something sleek, strange, and seriously messed up. The track moves through industrial, electronic, and nu-metal influences with a sleek sense of threat, all pressure points and polished unease. Working with producers Sean Beavan, whose resume includes Nine Inch Nails and 8mm, and Matt McJunkins of A Perfect Circle and Puscifer, Staytus lets S + M breathe inside a space built from serrated textures, heavy electronics, and vocals that shift between control and surrender. There is weight in the programming, but also a strange glamour to the way the song carries itself, like it knows obsession often looks better from a distance. Lyrically, “S + M” circles the afterlife of attachment: how someone can remain lodged in your identity even after distance has supposedly done its job. Desire becomes less a simple want than a feedback loop, intimate and magnetic, with every return carrying the faint humiliation of knowing better and reaching anyway. Directed by Vicente Cordero of Industrialism Films, the video initially shows how seduction gets more interesting when something feels slightly off. The clip begins in a place of closeness, teasing erotic tension and emotional dependency, then gradually tilts into psychological distortion. By the ending, the relationship at the center of the video has been rearranged in the viewer’s mind, less romance than a private fantasy gone rancid. A bold choice in these times. Staytus frames that narrative shift with precision: “I’ve always been inspired by films and visual storytelling that leave people unsettled in a beautiful way,” she says. “S + M starts off feeling seductive and emotionally intimate, but as the story unfolds, it becomes something much darker and more psychologically distorted. I wanted the ending to completely reframe the emotional experience of the song.” Watch the music video for Staytys’ “S + M” here: Follow Staytus: Facebook Instagram Spotify YouTube Bandcamp Website The post Los Angeles Alt-Industrial Artist Staytus Shares Video for Unsettling Thriller “S + M” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
